Your guide to the California Congressional District 40 race: Kim vs. Calvert

Republican incumbents Ken Calvert and Young Kim are facing off to keep their seats in Congress and represent California’s 40th District.

The seat, which blends portions of Calvert‘s and Kim’s current districts, reaches from Mission Viejo in Orange County into Woodcrest, Menifee and Murrieta in Riverside County.

California’s Hispanic Legislative Caucus hopes to hold the GOP line

Two years ago, Suzette Martinez Valladares and her fellow Latino Republicans made history in California.

They rode a Latino shift to the right during the 2024 presidential election and more than doubled the number of Latino Republican state legislators from four to nine. Valladares, who won her Antelope Valley state Senate race after previously serving in the Assembly, was inspired to co-found the California Hispanic Legislative Caucus with Assemblymember Kate Sanchez. They finally had their own caucus, since the 54-year-old California Latino Legislative Caucus has long barred Republicans from joining their clica.

The GOP group has since formed a political action committee, held listening sessions titled Escucha (“Listen Up”) across the state and launched a policy summit to hammer out a winnable platform, with Democrats holding all statewide seats as well as super-majorities in both legislative bodies. All Hispanic Legislative Caucus members won their primaries, and three of four candidates the group endorsed — Guillermo Gonzalez from the Central Valley for state Senate and Ed Delgado in the Inland Empire and Gracey Van Der Mark in Orange County for Assembly seats — moved on to the general election.

“I think our message resonates because Latino families want what other Californians want: a good job, a safe neighborhood, a good school for their kids and a home they can leave to the next generation,” Valladares told me as she and her group prepared for an unenviable midterm.

Every Latino GOP state legislator except Valladares and Rosilicie Ochoa Bogh (who’s not a member of the Hispanic caucus) is up for reelection in a year where the Republican Party is expected to lose control of Congress. Many Latinos seem to be forsaking the party after two years of mass deportations and a depressed economy under President Trump.

Van Der Mark, a Huntington Beach councilmember who has led Surf City’s MAGA turn over the past four years, is expected to win. But Gonzalez and Delgado face popular incumbents. Meanwhile, Inland Empire Assemblymembers Jeff Gonzalez (no relation to Guillermo) and Leticia Castillo face tough reelection bids after eking out victories two years ago, with Castillo winning by less than 600 votes.

Nevertheless, Valladares is “hopeful” that Latino GOP legislators will hold their gains.

“We earn that trust [with voters] between elections by showing up, listening and doing the work to put that California dream within reach,” she said.

History in Georgia and Florida as Bottoms, Donalds win gubernatorial races

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has defeated Republican Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor’s race, according to a projection by the Associated Press, to become the first Black woman elected governor in the nation’s history.

Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, is the first Democrat to win the Georgia governor’s seat in more than 20 years. She will be the first woman and first Black person to be elected to the seat.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds was projected to win the governor’s race, becoming that state’s first Black governor. Until tonight, only three Black governors had been elected by voters in U.S. history. One of them is Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, who was reelected Tuesday, according to an Associated Press projection.

Trump’s closing message to American voters highlights repairs to Reflecting Pool

WASHINGTON — After spending a month asking voters to treat the midterms as a vote on him, President Trump closed his monthlong campaign sprint on Monday sounding like a man bracing for defeat.

“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” Trump said. “But we gave this a very strong shot.”

Democrats secure one of four seat flips needed for Senate control

The Senate seat in North Carolina, won by the state’s former Gov. Roy Cooper, was the first Republican seat picked up by Democrats on Tuesday night, according to an early Associated Press projection.

Cooper won the seat being vacated by Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring after clashing repeatedly with President Trump.

Democrats must flip three more seats and hold all of their existing seats in order to gain control of the Senate.

In an acceptance speech, Cooper said chaos and corruption in Washington are harming North Carolinians. He said he will work to ease economic pain felt by residents of his state, including for healthcare, groceries and gas.

“I will put you before politics,” he said. “I will put you before party.”

Which races might predict a ‘blue wave’? Here’s what to watch

WASHINGTON — Americans are heading to the polls Tuesday in a historic set of midterm elections that will determine which party controls the chambers of Congress for the remainder of President Trump’s time in office.

Democrats appear poised to make significant gains, with polling showing the party up between 7 and 11 points on the generic ballot. Republicans are braced for losses but hoping to hang on to Senate control.

Even if DSA candidates lose tonight, the political thorn has already won

While the country watches to see whether a blue tsunami will flush out the GOP-held House and Senate, and Californians await the likely election of the state’s first Latino governor in modern times, Los Angeles will weather the latest round in a political battle royale that’s been going on this entire decade: How progressive is the city, truly?

In one corner is the city’s Democratic establishment, inheritors of the multicultural coalition that has run L.A. politics since Tom Bradley’s epochal mayoral win in 1973. They helped put Mayor Karen Bass in office four years ago and created the Black and Latino political machines now backing Jose Ugarte’s bid to replace his former boss, City Councilmember Curren Price, in District 9. They also supported Jimmy Gomez in 2017 when he ran to replace Xavier Becerra in Congress.

With Democrats holding a huge voter registration advantage in L.A. County — 51% versus 26% for Republicans, with 23% of voters choosing no party — the establishment should have built a forever regime, the way Democrats have in Sacramento. Instead, their thorn is the Democratic Socialists of America’s L.A. chapter, which will be able to declare victory in this election no matter what, thanks to the already strong showing of candidates they’ve endorsed.

Three incumbents — LAUSD trustee Rocio Rivas and L.A. City Councilmembers Eunisses Hernandez and Hugo Soto-Martínez — won outright in the June primary. In the Nov. 3 election, Bass is in a dead heat against Councilmember Nithya Raman, while a recent USC poll puts Angela Gonzales-Torres slightly ahead in the congressional race against Gomez, who’s dealing with a House Ethics Committee investigation into alleged sexual misconduct (he has denied everything). In the race for L.A. city attorney, Marissa Roy is easily ahead of her opponent, John McKinney, after incumbent Hydee Feldstein Soto failed to make the runoff.

The only place the establishment pick is resting easy is District 9, with Ugarte out-fundraising Estuardo Mazariegos and expected to become the first non-Black council member in 63 years to represent that part of South L.A.

Even if Bass and Gomez survive, the DSA will have shown, once again, that it’s not to be underestimated. If Raman or Gonzalez-Torres — or both? or even Mazariegos? — pull off upsets, expect the establishment to gnash its teeth over those pesky DSA kids, wearing their incisors down to nubs.

DSAers still won’t have full control of the clown car that’s L.A. politics, even in the best-case scenario — but they’ll be riding shotgun and raring to grab the wheel.

Your guide to the California state schools superintendent race: Barrera vs. Shaw

The office of state superintendent of public instruction is classified as nonpartisan, but that’s not how the candidates line up: Sonja Shaw is a conservative Republican whose views align closely with those of the Trump administration; Richard Barrera is a liberal Democrat backed by the California Teachers Assn. and closely aligned with its views.

They are vying for an office with little clear authority and an uncertain future. In June, the Legislature signed off on Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to reshape the position. By nearly all accounts, the state superintendent’s power has been reduced — and the authority of the office already was somewhat limited. Many of the new duties have yet to be worked out.

Late-counted votes likely to help Raman

Late-arriving mail-in ballots counted over the next few days are likely to favor Nithya Raman, so don’t take election night counts as the final word, experts say.

The ballots that are counted in the days after election day in L.A. historically skew toward younger, more progressive voters, said Paul Mitchell, who runs the voter data firm PDI.

Mitchell said he believes Bass needs a double-digit lead in the election day returns to consider herself safe from a Raman comeback.

Raman made significant gains in the mayoral primary after election day in June. She was trailing both Bass and Spencer Pratt the night of the election, but gained day after day on Pratt, eventually taking over the No. 2 spot.

Bass made up massive ground after election day against Rick Caruso in 2022, when she was the more left-wing candidate in the race.

Caruso led Bass by more than 2 percentage points in the early morning after election day that year, and Bass ended up winning the race by nearly 10 points.

“What is the demarcation line this year?” Mitchell wondered. “Bass did a 12-point move on Caruso; now will Nithya have to do a 12-point rout on Bass?”

Mitchell said that close watchers should also look out for how big the “undervote” is, meaning people who vote but decide to skip the mayor’s race on their ballots.

Those are likely to be Republican voters who can’t stomach either Democrat, Bass or Raman.

Since Bass performs better with Republicans, a smaller undervote would favor Bass, while more people choosing not to vote in the mayoral election would tend to favor Raman.

“The undervote is a metric for whether Republicans are voting. So when we get first returns, what does the undervote look like? If it’s low, Karen is potentially getting more Republican voters to plug their noses and vote for her.”

Florida Reps. Kathy Castor, Jared Moskowitz win reelection in Florida, a positive sign for Democrats amid redistricting

Democrats have a good sign in Florida’s 14th and 25th congressional districts, where Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz are projected to survive gerrymandering to hold their seats, according to the Associated Press.

The victories, which the Associated Press called just after 8 p.m. Eastern time, represents an early failure for the redistricting effort by state Republicans. Voters in the districts, which were redrawn for the 2026 election cycle, favored Republican Donald Trump for president in the last election, where voters in the prior district boundaries cast their ballots for Democrat Kamala Harris.

Polls have now closed in a large batch of states, including Texas and Maine, which are seen to be key states for determining the makeup of the Senate. They are also closed in Florida, a state where ballot-counting happens quickly — and so far, margins appear far slimmer in the red state than expected in some House races and in the Senate and gubernatorial races.

And in Denton County, Texas, which was a bellwether for the state’s support for Trump in the 2024 election, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico was ahead of Republican nominee Ken Paxton by nine points.

“Anything remotely like this … is what Democrats have been wishing they would see in places like this for decades now,” said NBC News analyst Steve Kornacki.

Chris Pappas wins Senate election in New Hampshire, holding Democratic seat

Chris Pappas, a Democratic congressman, has won New Hampshire’s open U.S. Senate seat, defeating Republican former Sen. John Sununu, according to a projection by the Associated Press.

Polls showed Pappas had a consistent lead in the race, which drew national attention as both parties competed for control of the Senate.

Sununu, who represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 to 2009, sought to reclaim his former seat after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced she would not seek reelection.

Democrats had hoped to hold the New Hampshire seat as part of their effort to win control of the Senate. Pappas’ victory preserves a Democratic-held seat, keeping the party’s path to a Senate majority alive.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, wins Senate race

Roy Cooper, the Democratic former governor of North Carolina, has won election to the seat being vacated by Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.

Cooper was governor from 2017 to 2025 and attorney general before that. He won both races for governor in years when President Trump carried the state in the presidential race. Now he’s the first Democrat elected by North Carolina voters since 2008.

Challenging Cooper was Michael Whatley, former chair of the national and state Republican parties who was endorsed by Trump and never had run for public office.

Cooper’s win brings Democrats closer to tilting the balance of power in the Senate. He outraised Whatley by nearly $36 million, according to the Associated Press.

The race was seen as a proving ground for whether association with Trump is a benefit or a liability in the current political climate. With voters increasingly worried about the economy, Republicans in other battleground states sought to distance themselves from the president. Tillis announced his retirement after clashing repeatedly with Trump, including over concerns about his major tax and spending package and certain Cabinet nominees.

Cooper campaigned on affordability; his platform slogan was “Make stuff cost less.”

Final hours of 2026 midterm voting: A procrastinator’s guide

We’ve reached the final hours for voting in California, but there’s still time to cast your ballot in the midterm election.

Here’s what you need to know on election day.

A fight for O.C.’s Latino political soul in the state’s most expensive legislative race

I live in California’s 68th Assembly District, which covers most of Anaheim and Santa Ana and part of Orange and is the scene of the most expensive legislative race in the state this year. That means candidates Jessie Lopez and David Penaloza have basically lived in my house since the spring.

Television and YouTube ads. Mailers that clutter both my P.O. box and my regular mailbox. Friends of mine campaigning and donating. The candidates — both Democrats and members of the Santa Ana City Council — doing meet-and-greets at my wife’s downtown Santa Ana store.

One mailer even included an ex-girlfriend of mine who’s a Lopez supporter, yet somehow ended up in an attack ad against her!

That’s what happens when more than $15 million in independent expenditures pours into a seat that’s been safely Democratic for nearly 30 years. Tech bros and real estate and oil companies have dumped over $12 million to praise the moderate Penaloza and trash the progressive Lopez, who is relying on unions for her relatively miserly haul of $3.5 million.

Why so much money spent on a working-class Latino district? Because it’s a microcosm of the Democratic Party’s battle for the Latino soul of Orange County — again.

In 2022, I wrote about the 68th’s two hopefuls at the time: Anaheim City Councilmember Avelino Valencia, a moderate, and Bulmaro “Boomer” Vicente, a progressive. Valencia handily won, continuing a long Orange County tradition of moderate Latinos beating their progressive primos.

Democratic Latinos like Valencia seized a majority on the Anaheim City Council and took the upper hand in Santa Ana, and Valencia is expected to easily win his bid for the 34th Senate District.

But Vicente didn’t completely lose: With friends, he regrouped to engineer a progressive counter-revolution.

They helped Lopez beat back a 2023 recall and assisted Orange County Supervisor Vicente Sarmiento in winning outright in the June primary. They are now organizing the campaigns of Lopez and Santa Ana Unified School District trustee Hector Bustos, as well as Santa Ana City Council candidates Isuri Ramos and Sandra de Anda — all native santaneros.

The Latino Dem-versus-Latino Dem centrist-leftist free-for-all mirrors similar battles across California, from the Imperial Valley to the Central Valley, L.A.’s Eastside to the Inland Empire. But it hits different in a place like Orange County, which is becoming more and more purple and is seeing more Latinos win in cities with small Latino communities like Irvine and Mission Viejo. If Penaloza wins, that keeps centrist Latinos in power.

If Lopez wins?

Watch out, L.A.: This ain’t Loretta Sanchez’s O.C. anymore.

Your guide to the California Congressional District 45 race: Tran vs. Vo

Incumbent Derek Tran is attempting to win the district that centers around Little Saigon for a second consecutive time.

Tran was a political newcomer when he captured the seat by a little more than 600 votes in 2024 against Michelle Steel, a two-time incumbent Republican. He’ll face off against Republican Chuong Vo, a recently retired Torrance police officer.

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff keeps his seat in Georgia race

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has staved off his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, to keep his Senate seat in the Georgia race, according to an Associated Press projection.

Ossoff’s win is welcome news for Democrats, who are seeking to take back the Senate majority from Republicans after President Trump won Georgia by 2 percentage points in 2024.

The incumbent’s campaign messaging focused on the economy as he criticized the Trump administration for tariffs, inflation and the Iran war. Collins, meanwhile, blamed inflation on the Biden administration.

As the election neared, some Republicans began to view the Georgia race as less competitive than anticipated, with Collins lagging behind Ossoff in polls.

Your guide to the California insurance commissioner race: Allen vs. Kim

The race to succeed Ricardo Lara as California insurance commissioner following the devastating January 2025 wildfires is a classic study in contrasts.

It pits a veteran legislator, state Sen. Ben Allen (D-Santa Monica), serving his third and final term in the  Senate, against an upstart progressive candidate, Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor. They topped a packed field of candidates in the June 2 primary.

Exit polls show widespread voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s policies, economy and the war in Iran

Voters are expressing a sharp split with President Trump on his policies, according to multiple exit polls.

About three-quarters of voters in the AP Voter Poll said they were “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory, and about the same proportion had negative views about the economy’s condition.

Six in 10 in the AP poll signaled unhappiness with the Trump administration’s immigration policies and with the war in Iran. About two-thirds of voters told CNN that Trump’s tariff policies had harmed their local economies.

And 43% in the NBC News Exit Poll said they viewed voting as a chance to express opposition to Trump, a higher share than those who said the same in the midterm election during Trump’s first term.

Trump rages at Fox News poll ahead of polls closing

President Trump, while watching Fox News’ election night coverage from the White House, lashed out at a poll showing voters were unhappy with his handling of the economy and the direction of the country.

In a post on social media, Trump called the Fox News poll “so insulting with the questions they ask.” He added: “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is BULL—! This has been going on for years.”

It was not clear which questions and responses Trump was referring to. The survey asked voters their thoughts on the economy and whether Trump’s policies had made life more affordable, among other topics.

The responses were largely unfavorable to the president.

Your guide to the California Congressional District 34 race: Gomez vs. Gonzales-Torres

Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Los Angeles) has successfully beaten back reelection challenges from the left over  nearly a decade in Congress.

This year, powerful progressive groups, including Justice Democrats,  are coalescing behind candidate Angela Gonzales-Torres, a Highland Park resident who served on the area’s neighborhood council.

Busy USC Village polling center runs out of ‘I Voted’ stickers

Vote centers opened at 7 a.m. Tuesday, but a line formed long before then at USC Village.

“The line started at 6:15 a.m.,” said Sergio Bravo, lead poll worker for the polling place.

Bravo said the center has been busy all day.

“We have a great team,” he said. “We’ve been able to keep the line going nonstop.”

It’s been so busy that the polling place ran out of “I Voted” stickers.

Another poll worker said the polling place may have to remain open well past 8 p.m. to accommodate everyone standing in the growing line.

In California, any voter who is in line at 8 p.m. when the polls are scheduled to close is allowed to vote, according to the secretary of state.

If there is a line when the polls close, a poll worker stands at the back to let people who arrive after 8 p.m. know that they are no longer able to join the queue.

Jeffries expresses confidence in Democrats’ chances to retake House

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries projected confidence about his party’s chances of retaking control of the chamber ahead of polls closing on Tuesday night.

“The early vote numbers were strong, and today’s vote numbers all across the country are strong in blue states, in swing states and in red states,” the New York Democrat told reporters in Washington. “But ultimately, this is in the hands of the American people.”

Jeffries said he was particularly watching the result in Kentucky’s 6th District, a Republican stronghold that could be in play this year.

Your guide to the California secretary of state race: Weber vs. Wagner

California voters will decide this November whether incumbent Shirley Weber will be reelected as secretary of state of California or her challenger, Republican Don Wagner, will replace her.

The secretary of state is in charge of administering statewide elections, providing information about ballot measures and candidates to voters and overseeing campaign financing. The office also handles business licensing and filings.

Democrats and Republicans watching congressional races in Kentucky and Indiana for early predictions

The nation’s first polls have now closed in Kentucky and Indiana, and both parties are watching congressional race returns closely.

Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District is likely to be the earliest sign of how well Democrats may do tonight. If Democrat Zach Dembo beats Republican Ralph Alvarado in the race for the seat, which is currently held by outgoing GOP Rep. Andy Barr, that will bolster Democratic hopes as the night continues.

Barr is running for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.)

Billionaire tax nearly shatters California campaign finance records — with billionaires spending the most

Spending on the proposed tax on billionaires’ assets nearly shattered California campaign finance records, with $425 million donated to three ballot measures supporting and opposing the effort.

In state history, the only issue that received more campaign contributions was gambling proposals on the 2022 ballot, which received $463.4 million in donations.

The billionaire tax, Proposition 40, was crafted by a healthcare union to compensate for impending federal healthcare cuts expected to cost California $100 billion and impact the state’s most vulnerable residents.

Two other proposals — Propositions 41 and 42 — were written by opponents of the measure. Opponents of Proposition 40 and supporters of the two measures designed to nullify it raised the vast majority of money in the contest, mostly from the state’s billionaires — $388.4 million as of Tuesday, according to the secretary of state’s office.

Supporters of Proposition 40 raised $36.6 million, but much of it was spent gathering signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot prior to the June primary.

The end result has been evident in the closing weeks of the campaign — supporters of the billionaire tax have relied on media coverage of events such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) rallying for its passage, while voters have been inundated by television ads during Sunday NFL games, cooking shows and elsewhere, opposing it or supporting the counter proposals.

Consultant for Bass’ mayoral campaign under fire for questionable Instagram post

A consultant for Karen Bass’ mayoral campaign has come under fire for an Instagram post cautioning voters not to cast their ballots based on “ethnic sounding last names.”

The election day post by Jasmyne Cannick, which was later removed, included a voter guide instructing people to read candidates’ platforms and look at their records. “We are not voting off vibes, catchy slogans, or ethnic sounding last names,” it read in bold text.

Some took offense at the remark, which the Bass campaign also condemned.

“I was shocked that someone so closely related to the campaign would say something like that,” said Rutik Shinglot, who serves as treasurer of the Westside Young Democrats and volunteered as a door knocker for the campaign of Bass’ opponent, Nithya Raman. He said his remarks represented his personal views only, not those of the Young Democrats.

“I’ve never really had someone that looks like me do what Nithya’s trying to do,” said Shinglot, who, like Raman, is South Asian. He said he found her mayoral run inspiring and efforts to tear her down offensive.

“I have thick skin so I can look past it,” he said. “But for folks who are trying to get into politics and have their voices heard, it really is discouraging.”

Cannick did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. Bass’ reelection campaign has paid her $20,000 for consulting services, campaign finance records state.

“We strongly condemn the language in this post,” said Alex Stack, a spokesperson for Bass’ campaign. “It was made in her individual capacity and was not authorized by the campaign, and it has been removed.”

Raman’s campaign denounced the language. “Los Angeles is a city of immigrants, and we reject the Bass campaign’s divisive, xenophobic rhetoric,” spokesperson Liz Garcia wrote in a statement. “This is a shameful way for Bass’ campaign to close this election.”

Cannick later reposted the voter guide, replacing “ethnic sounding last names” with “Black sounding names.”

“In all my years of posting my voter guide, I have NEVER had to take it down and put it back up because somebody manufactured an issue where there wasn’t one,” she wrote in the caption. “But I guess the Nithya Defense League wasn’t previously staffed to scrutinize my every post, word, and punctuation mark.

“For the record: I can see how they misunderstood what I said when taking it outside of the context of the Black community of which it was meant for,” she continued.

“In my experience as a Black person, conversations in the Black community about voting for judges regularly include how some of us Black people pick a last name that sounds familiar instead of researching who we’re electing. In almost all my previous voter guides, I’ve poked fun at that in a petty, funny way to say: We as Black people are NOT doing that this election. We’re doing our homework.”

Shinglot responded via text message that he’s glad Cannick changed the language. “Whatever the intent, framing this election around whose last name sounds ‘ethnic’ pits communities of color against each other at the exact moment we need to be standing together,” he added.

Your guide to L.A. City Charter Amendment EE: City Council meetings, ethics and elections

Most Los Angeles City Council members would rather not be required to meet three days a week. But for that to happen, they will need to get permission from their bosses — that is, the city’s voters.

Amendment EE on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the council to meet once a week instead of three times, as now required under the city charter. The council voted 12-0 to put the measure on the ballot, with Councilmembers Heather Hutt, Curren Price and Monica Rodriguez absent.

Your guide to Proposition 39: Stricter voter ID requirements

Proposition 39 brings the national debate around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter ID requirements for state elections — mandating that voters present government identification every time they vote in person, or cite a specific government ID number when voting by mail.

The measure is backed by prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump, who is pushing even more onerous voter ID measures at the national level. The measure’s backers say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. They contend, without evidence, that such problems are widespread in California.

The L.A. mayoral election is today — who are these celebrities voting for?

Today’s the day, and the race is a dead heat: The final poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (co-sponsored by The Times) found that 40% of likely L.A. voters supported incumbent Karen Bass, while another 40% supported progressive challenger Nithya Raman for L.A. mayor.

That leaves 19% undecided — and it might be those voters that celebrities are trying to reach with their recent endorsements. Jane Fonda, Yvette Nicole Brown, Anthony Anderson, Cedric the Entertainer, Samuel L. Jackson, Kym Whitley, D.L. Hughley, Dustin Lance Black, George Lopez and Stevie Wonder  all voiced public support for Bass. Meanwhile Bob Odenkirk, Mindy Kaling, Adam Scott, Joel Kim Booster, Caleb Hearon, Poppy Liu, P. J. Byrne, Adam Conover, Brennan Lee Mulligan and Jaboukie Young-White have done the same for Raman.

Voter turnout exceeds typical midterms, notably among young Latino voters

Nearly 6.5 million Californians — more than a quarter of the state’s registered voters — had cast ballots before today’s election. That’s 1.4 million more than in the last midterm election in 2022.

The party controlling the White House typically loses congressional seats during a midterm election, and while current voting trends align with this pattern, a notable shift is the uptick of Latino and young voters who have voted early, according to Paul Mitchell, a veteran Democratic strategist who specializes in analysis of voting trends.

Mitchell estimated that there will be 4 million to 6 million outstanding ballots that are likely being cast by young voters, who are more likely to support the proposed tax on the assets of billionaires (Proposition 40), Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman, and insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim, while opposing the voter ID mandate (Proposition 39).

“Young Latinos … go from being 5.5% of turnout in 2022 to 10.3% now. It’s almost double,” he said, notably in the Inland Empire and the Central Valley.

One of the largest surges of Latino voters is in the congressional district of Rep. David Valadao (R-Hanford), whom Democrats have been trying to topple for years. Though their party’s voters outnumber Republicans in the district, Valadao has hung on to the seat partly because of his connection with his constituents.

Republican candidates eked out narrow wins in Florida’s gubernatorial and Senate races Tuesday, raising the question of whether Florida has reverted to being a swing state.

Republican Florida Rep. Byron Donalds, the state’s GOP gubernatorial nominee, won a closer-than-expected race to succeed term-limited Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. He bested Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former GOP congressman, 50.0% to 48.7% with more than 95% of ballots counted, according to The Associated Press (AP). The close call comes just two years after President Donald Trump carried the Sunshine State by 13 percentage points and four years after DeSantis won reelection in a nearly 20-point landslide.

Donalds’s victory marks the eighth consecutive time the Republican nominee won a Florida gubernatorial election. He will also be the first black Republican governor in American history.

The congressman, who has represented a deep-red seat based in Fort Myers and Naples since 2020, won a contested August primary with Trump’s backing, receiving 47.8% of the vote, according to AP. Republican Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, with 25.2% of the vote, came in a distant second place while 31-year-old investor James Fishback — who had significant support among young voters — came in third with 10.5% of the vote.

Donalds told Daily Caller Editor-in-Chief Amber Duke in September that Fishback drew votes from many Gen Z Floridians who saw hope for their future symbolized in him.

“I think if anything resonated, it is that young people want to know that there’s a plan for their success,” the congressman told Duke. “Whether you’re going to college or not going to college, we want to make sure every child in our state, every young adult in our state, has a chance to build, you know, the Florida dream for themselves.”

Angie Nixon during a campaign event at the St. John Missionary Baptist Church on September 28, 2026 in Boynton Beach, Florida. Jolly is running against Republican gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL) for the Florida governorship in the November 3rd election. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Donalds also told Duke he supports certain guardrails on data centers, in contrast to Jolly, who promised he would immediately place a moratorium on data center construction in the Sunshine State, likely for a full year.

“When it comes to energy and electricity bills, we are very clear in our state that a data center is not going to raise the utility costs of Floridians,” he said, adding that the centers should also recycle the water they use and not be in close proximity to residential areas. “My position is, if you’re not going to protect our resources and you’re not going to protect people’s utility bills, then no data centers.”Regarding the increased deployment of Flock Safety cameras in local communities, the congressman said the “Fourth Amendment is not up for debate on this.” “We don’t want to have people feeling like they’re being surveilled by some private company, or even being surveilled by their government,” he added. “That’s not going to take place in our state.”

Before becoming Florida’s anti-data center Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Jolly represented a St. Petersburg-based House district as a moderate Republican from 2013 to 2017. Less than two years after losing reelection, he left the Republican Party, citing his criticism of Trump. He joined the Democratic Party and announced his run for governor in 2025.

At the same time, Republican Florida Sen. Ashley Moody won her special election, beating surprise Democratic nominee state Rep. Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member from Jacksonville. The incumbent senator received 50.9% of the vote to Nixon’s 48.0% with more than 95% of ballots counted, AP reported.

DeSantis had appointed Moody — then Florida’s attorney general — to replace Marco Rubio, who resigned in January 2025 after being confirmed as the U.S. secretary of state. Since Tuesday’s race was merely a special election to complete what would have been Rubio’s term, Moody will face reelection again in 2028.

Nixon had won her Aug. 18 Democratic primary in an upset, decisively beating heavily favored retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman, a Ukrainian immigrant and key figure from Trump’s first impeachment. Running to his left, Nixon beat Vindman by double digits despite being outspent 16 to 1.

While Florida Democrats suffered significant losses during the 2022 and 2024 election cycles, the state party appeared to roar back in spring 2026 with two state legislative special election wins in a pair of seats that voted for Trump.

Florida’s presidential vote was notably decided by single digits in every race from 1992 to 2020.

Your guide to the California Congressional District 40 race: Kim vs. Calvert

Republican incumbents Ken Calvert and Young Kim are facing off to keep their seats in Congress and represent California’s 40th District.

California’s Hispanic Legislative Caucus hopes to hold the GOP line

Two years ago, Suzette Martinez Valladares and her fellow Latino Republicans made history in California.

They rode a Latino shift to the right during the 2024 presidential election and more than doubled the number of Latino Republican state legislators from four to nine. Valladares, who won her Antelope Valley state Senate race after previously serving in the Assembly, was inspired to co-found the California Hispanic Legislative Caucus with Assemblymember Kate Sanchez. They finally had their own caucus, since the 54-year-old California Latino Legislative Caucus has long barred Republicans from joining their clica.

The GOP group has since formed a political action committee, held listening sessions titled Escucha (“Listen Up”) across the state and launched a policy summit to hammer out a winnable platform, with Democrats holding all statewide seats as well as super-majorities in both legislative bodies. All Hispanic Legislative Caucus members won their primaries, and three of four candidates the group endorsed — Guillermo Gonzalez from the Central Valley for state Senate and Ed Delgado in the Inland Empire and Gracey Van Der Mark in Orange County for Assembly seats — moved on to the general election.

“I think our message resonates because Latino families want what other Californians want: a good job, a safe neighborhood, a good school for their kids and a home they can leave to the next generation,” Valladares told me as she and her group prepared for an unenviable midterm.

Every Latino GOP state legislator except Valladares and Rosilicie Ochoa Bogh (who’s not a member of the Hispanic caucus) is up for reelection in a year where the Republican Party is expected to lose control of Congress. Many Latinos seem to be forsaking the party after two years of mass deportations and a depressed economy under President Trump.

Van Der Mark, a Huntington Beach councilmember who has led Surf City’s MAGA turn over the past four years, is expected to win. But Gonzalez and Delgado face popular incumbents. Meanwhile, Inland Empire Assemblymembers Jeff Gonzalez (no relation to Guillermo) and Leticia Castillo face tough reelection bids after eking out victories two years ago, with Castillo winning by less than 600 votes.

Nevertheless, Valladares is “hopeful” that Latino GOP legislators will hold their gains.

“We earn that trust [with voters] between elections by showing up, listening and doing the work to put that California dream within reach,” she said.

History in Georgia and Florida as Bottoms, Donalds win gubernatorial races

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has defeated Republican Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor’s race, according to a projection by the Associated Press, to become the first Black woman elected governor in the nation’s history.

Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, is the first Democrat to win the Georgia governor’s seat in more than 20 years. She will be the first woman and first Black person to be elected to the seat.

Becerra urges voters not to be intimidated by Trump’s election interference threats

Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra sought to reassure California voters that it was safe to vote in Tuesday’s election in light of the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on the state’s voting process.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and others have warned that President Trump could seek to intervene in the midterm election and potentially attempt to seize ballots.

After voting in Sacramento, Becerra said  voters might notice volunteers working at polling stations in California to ensure that no one is intimidated.

“We want to see record numbers [of voters turn out], we want to fight back against that intimidation, that obstruction,” Becerra added.

Becerra told reporters  “we have seen this movie before — it was a C-rated movie,” a reference to  Trump’s past efforts to scrutinize California’s elections.

Trump claimed, without evidence last week, that “there are hundreds of thousands of bad ballots, bad votes, in California. Millions, in my opinion.”

In mid-October, the Trump administration sued California and said federal courts should require California and Los Angeles County to “set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the federal government likely to be noncitizens.”

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday turned down the Trump administration’s bid to set aside ballots from 20,000 California voters who the administration alleges may not be citizens.

The litigation has been met with deep concern from state leaders.

“It’s a sad statement that we can’t depend on our own federal government to have our backs,” Becerra said.

Seven hundred and twenty-eight days ago, Americans handed Donald Trump’s Republican Party complete control of the US government. Two years later, voters declared they’d had enough. On Tuesday, Democrats decisively won control of the House of Representatives, putting an end to the president’s ability to govern the country with essentially zero resistance or oversight from the legislative branch.

Democrats won key races across the country, prevailing in districts from Florida to North Carolina to Kentucky.

Trump’s second term has been among the most destructive and most corrupt periods in modern American political history, thanks in large part to congressional Republicans’ near total disinterest in pushing back on his unprecedented abuses of power. On issues ranging from militarized immigration enforcement to ruinous tariffs, the House GOP has enabled one Trumpian calamity after another.

Tuesday’s result won’t put an end to the president’s ability to wreak havoc across the globe, but it will enable Democrats to push back far more effectively against the administration. They will now have far more authority to hold hearings, compel testimony, and subpoena documents, as well as to derail Trump’s legislative agenda, control federal spending, extract policy concessions, and—critically—exercise oversight and launch investigations of the administration’s misdeeds.

Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images

Republican candidates eked out narrow wins in Florida’s gubernatorial and Senate races Tuesday, raising the question of whether Florida has reverted to being a swing state.

Republican Florida Rep. Byron Donalds, the state’s GOP gubernatorial nominee, won a closer-than-expected race to succeed term-limited Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. He bested Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former GOP congressman, 50.0% to 48.7% with more than 95% of ballots counted, according to The Associated Press (AP). The close call comes just two years after President Donald Trump carried the Sunshine State by 13 percentage points and four years after DeSantis won reelection in a nearly 20-point landslide.

Donalds’s victory marks the eighth consecutive time the Republican nominee won a Florida gubernatorial election. He will also be the first black Republican governor in American history.

The congressman, who has represented a deep-red seat based in Fort Myers and Naples since 2020, won a contested August primary with Trump’s backing, receiving 47.8% of the vote, according to AP. Republican Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, with 25.2% of the vote, came in a distant second place while 31-year-old investor James Fishback — who had significant support among young voters — came in third with 10.5% of the vote.

Donalds told Daily Caller Editor-in-Chief Amber Duke in September that Fishback drew votes from many Gen Z Floridians who saw hope for their future symbolized in him.

“I think if anything resonated, it is that young people want to know that there’s a plan for their success,” the congressman told Duke. “Whether you’re going to college or not going to college, we want to make sure every child in our state, every young adult in our state, has a chance to build, you know, the Florida dream for themselves.”

BOYNTON BEACH, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 28: Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon during a campaign event at the St. John Missionary Baptist Church on September 28, 2026 in Boynton Beach, Florida. Jolly is running against Republican gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL) for the Florida governorship in the November 3rd election. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Donalds also told Duke he supports certain guardrails on data centers, in contrast to Jolly, who promised he would immediately place a moratorium on data center construction in the Sunshine State, likely for a full year.

“When it comes to energy and electricity bills, we are very clear in our state that a data center is not going to raise the utility costs of Floridians,” he said, adding that the centers should also recycle the water they use and not be in close proximity to residential areas. “My position is, if you’re not going to protect our resources and you’re not going to protect people’s utility bills, then no data centers.”Regarding the increased deployment of Flock Safety cameras in local communities, the congressman said the “Fourth Amendment is not up for debate on this.” “We don’t want to have people feeling like they’re being surveilled by some private company, or even being surveilled by their government,” he added. “That’s not going to take place in our state.”

Before becoming Florida’s anti-data center Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Jolly represented a St. Petersburg-based House district as a moderate Republican from 2013 to 2017. Less than two years after losing reelection, he left the Republican Party, citing his criticism of Trump. He joined the Democratic Party and announced his run for governor in 2025.

At the same time, Republican Florida Sen. Ashley Moody won her special election, beating surprise Democratic nominee state Rep. Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member from Jacksonville. The incumbent senator received 50.9% of the vote to Nixon’s 48.0% with more than 95% of ballots counted, AP reported.

DeSantis had appointed Moody — then Florida’s attorney general — to replace Marco Rubio, who resigned in January 2025 after being confirmed as the U.S. secretary of state. Since Tuesday’s race was merely a special election to complete what would have been Rubio’s term, Moody will face reelection again in 2028.

Nixon had won her Aug. 18 Democratic primary in an upset, decisively beating heavily favored retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman, a Ukrainian immigrant and key figure from Trump’s first impeachment. Running to his left, Nixon beat Vindman by double digits despite being outspent 16 to 1.

While Florida Democrats suffered significant losses during the 2022 and 2024 election cycles, the state party appeared to roar back in spring 2026 with two state legislative special election wins in a pair of seats that voted for Trump.

Florida’s presidential vote was notably decided by single digits in every race from 1992 to 2020.
